summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between statutory rights and their exercise is the main turbulence factor here. French law delivers marriage, anti-discrimination cover and simplified legal gender change, but reporting on the island documents delays and difficulty in reaching those entitlements in practice, and the local legal market offers little immediate help: a lawyer directory returns no referenced practitioner for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi or Sada, while a Paris-based lawyer before the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, is listed as available.

Detention remains the sharpest documented risk for trans people under French jurisdiction. The CGLPL's 2021 opinion describes systematic failures rather than isolated incidents, based on a decade of referrals, and no source in the inventory records any correction specific to overseas establishments.
localsOnly:
Residents may use the simplified legal gender-change procedure adopted by the National Assembly, which applies in Mayotte as French law; the same civil-status machinery governs marriage and name changes at the island's town halls.

Residents needing counsel on gender recognition, family matters or discrimination must look off-island: the lawyer directory lists no referenced practitioner in Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada or the other town queries, and points instead to a Paris-based lawyer admitted before the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation.

Local social conditions shape how rights are used. Reporting from Mayotte describes couples pursuing marriage through a long and complicated process on a predominantly Muslim island, and legal advocacy or social support structures for trans residents are not documented in the sources available here.
outOfScopeNotes:
The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 is national in scope and does not name Mayotte's establishments; whether any inspection or referral has covered a Mayotte facility is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory records a trans person actually detained on Mayotte, the conditions of the island's own jail, or how the Article D248 placement rule has been applied locally. The risk assessment transfers the national pattern rather than reporting a local case.

Whether the prefectoral authority on Mayotte issues identity documents with a changed gender marker on the same terms as metropolitan prefectures is not sourced in this inventory.

The 1975 date for the vote to remain part of France, and the characterisation of same-sex marriage as rare in Africa and the Islamic world, come from a single advocacy-site source and are not corroborated here by an official record.

The absence of a referenced LGBT-friendly lawyer in Mayotte reflects one directory's listings; it is not evidence that no practitioner on the island would take such a case.

No source addresses hate-crime charges, discrimination complaints or official hostility directed at trans people on Mayotte specifically.
